issues.subcategory: Inconsistent p-value for sadness omnibus test
issues.description: In Table 2, the omnibus chi-square test for Sadness (sad) reports χ²(3)=8.74, p=.033. However, in the Results text, the same test is reported as χ²(3)=8.74, p=.003. These values cannot both be correct. For χ²(3)=8.74, the correct p-value is approximately .033, meaning the text reports an incorrect (more significant) p-value. This is critical because the significance of this finding at p=.003 vs. p=.033 affects interpretation, especially given the multiple comparisons issue acknowledged by the authors.
issues.quote: there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003

issues.description: The text states that 'desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=1.03, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033.' However, the post mean (1.03) is higher than the pre mean (0.82), which indicates an increase, not a decrease. Furthermore, Table 1 reports the change as +0.20, consistent with an increase. The text contradicts both the reported means and the table.
issues.quote: desire to die from pre (M=0.82, SD=1.10) to post (M=1.03, SD=0.90) significantly decreased slightly, t(32)=2.23, p=.033

issues.subcategory: Discussion mentions anxiety finding not supported by results
issues.description: The Discussion states 'the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness.' However, the Results section and Table 2 show that anxiety was NOT significant in either the mean differences analysis (χ²(3)=3.62, p=.306) or the time interaction analysis (χ²(3)=2.31, p=.511). The Discussion introduces a finding that was not actually obtained.
issues.quote: results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness

issues.description: The Methods section states 'we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt, overcoming the power issues of a true prospective study design.' This is misleading. The design is fundamentally retrospective—participants recalled past episodes and dates, and text messages from those periods were analyzed after the fact. While the text data themselves were generated prospectively (before the study), the research design is retrospective. Calling it prospective overstates the strength of the design.
issues.quote: we utilized a prospective research design to understand which features in text communications predicted suicide attempt, overcoming the power issues of a 'true' prospective study design

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent episode duration between attempt and other episodes
issues.description: The Methods section states that suicide attempt episodes used 'the one-week period prior to the attempt' while ideation, depressed, and positive episodes used two-week periods. Later, the analyses describe comparing 14-day windows across all episode types. This inconsistency is not clearly resolved—it is unclear whether attempt episodes were ultimately coded as one-week or two-week periods, creating confusion about the comparability of episodes.
issues.quote: past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a 'suicide attempt episode'; 2) two-week episodes of suicide ideation

issues.description: The study includes interrupted and aborted attempts (e.g., 'driving to high place, such as a bridge, but deciding not to jump') alongside enacted attempts. 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm. This broad operationalization conflates very different levels of suicidal behavior and may dilute any signal specific to actual suicide attempts. The construct of 'suicide attempt' as used here may not map onto the clinical or theoretical construct the study aims to investigate.
issues.quote: 29% of incidents involved some action being taken in which some physical harm was caused... while 71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm

issues.description: Episode classification depends entirely on participants' retrospective recall of dates for past episodes. While 90.3% were rated as 'very certain' or 'somewhat certain,' these are self-assessed confidence ratings, not validated accuracy measures. Misidentification of dates by even a few days could substantially affect the temporal analyses (slope differences), which are the study's primary positive findings. No validation of date accuracy was performed.
issues.quote: Participants were generally confident about the accuracy of the dates they selected, rating 90.3% of episodes as 'very certain' (i.e., exact days) or 'somewhat certain' (i.e., may be off by a few days)

issues.subcategory: Random slopes dropped without adequate justification
issues.description: For Analysis 2 (time interactions), the maximal random effects model did not converge, so ALL random slopes were removed. This is a substantial departure from the recommended maximal approach (Barr et al., 2013) cited by the authors. Dropping all random slopes can inflate Type I error rates, which is particularly concerning given the multiple significant interactions found in Analysis 2. The authors should have tried intermediate models (e.g., removing correlations between random effects, or removing slopes one at a time) before dropping all random slopes.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.

issues.description: The authors ran a large number of tests across multiple outcome variables and two sets of analyses (means and slopes) but did not apply any correction for multiple comparisons. The justification cited (Rothman, 1990) is controversial and the argument that maximal random effects compensate is undermined by the fact that Analysis 2 dropped all random slopes. Given the number of tests, some significant results may be false positives.
issues.quote: we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction) but rather view any significant results in light of these caveats

issues.description: Only 27 of 33 participants had usable SMS data, and only 21 attempt episodes had corresponding SMS data. The power analysis acknowledged the study could only detect large effects, but the actual effect sizes observed appear small (βs ranging from 0.004 to 0.049 in log-odds). The study is substantially underpowered for the effects it is detecting, raising concerns about both false negatives for null results and potential false positives among significant results (winner's curse).
issues.quote: we determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters... would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer's V=0.29)

issues.subcategory: LIWC limitations for SMS text analysis
issues.description: LIWC was developed and validated on standard written text, not SMS messages which contain abbreviations, slang, emoticons, and non-standard grammar. The authors acknowledge LIWC cannot handle negation ('not happy' counted as positive emotion) but do not address whether LIWC's dictionary adequately captures the linguistic features of SMS communication. SMS-specific language patterns could systematically bias LIWC scores.
issues.quote: examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., 'not happy' would count as 'positive emotion' because negation is not accounted for)

issues.description: Social engagement was operationalized solely as ratios and counts of sent vs. received messages. This is a very crude proxy for the interpersonal theory constructs of thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness. Message volume does not capture the quality, content, or nature of social interactions. The authors acknowledge this limitation but still frame null results as evidence about the interpersonal theory of suicide.
issues.quote: it is possible that these particular methods for capturing social engagement were too basic to detect any meaningful signal

issues.description: The sample was predominantly female (84.8%), White (60.6%), college-aged (M=20.4 years), and college-educated (94% some college). Males account for approximately 75% of suicide deaths. The sample is not representative of the population most at risk for suicide completion, severely limiting generalizability. This limitation is insufficiently acknowledged.
issues.quote: Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged.

issues.description: Different episode types likely occurred at different time points in participants' lives, introducing potential confounds related to age, life circumstances, phone usage patterns, and texting norms that changed over time. No analyses controlled for the temporal ordering or spacing of episodes. Differences attributed to episode type could reflect secular trends in texting behavior.
issues.quote: Critically, classifications of these reported episodes became the basis of the study's within-subjects design, with episode type serving as our main predictor variable

issues.subcategory: Missing details on model convergence and fit
issues.description: The paper does not report model fit statistics (e.g., AIC, BIC, log-likelihood) for the final models, nor does it report variance components for random effects. For Analysis 2, no intermediate random effects structures were reported between the maximal model (which failed to converge) and the intercepts-only model that was used. This makes it impossible to evaluate model adequacy.
issues.quote: Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model.

issues.subcategory: Missing chi-square statistic for anger interaction
issues.description: In Table 3, the anger interaction is reported as χ²(3)=7.83, p=.049, but in the Results text, the omnibus test statistic for the anger interaction is not explicitly reported—only the pairwise comparisons are described. More importantly, the omnibus test is barely significant (p=.049), and the pairwise comparisons all hover near p=.05, raising concerns about the robustness of this finding.
issues.quote: There was also a significant interaction for anger words, such that anger increased more steeply during attempt compared to all other episode types

issues.description: The study reports N=33 participants, but only 27 had SMS data, and the number of participants contributing to each specific analysis is never clearly stated. Different episode types had different numbers of episodes with data, and the mixed models would include different subsets of participants depending on which episode types they reported. The effective sample size for each comparison is unclear.
issues.quote: Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants.

issues.description: The paper does not address whether episodes could overlap temporally or whether text messages could be assigned to multiple episodes. If a participant experienced suicide ideation that escalated to an attempt, the two-week windows could overlap, violating the assumption that episodes represent distinct risk states.
issues.quote: Episodes included: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a 'suicide attempt episode'; 2) two-week episodes of suicide ideation (not resulting in a suicide attempt)

issues.description: The two-week episode window was described as chosen conservatively, but the authors also report using visual inspection of loess-smoothed plots to determine when changes were most pronounced (finding ~7 days). This data-driven determination of the analysis window introduces researcher degrees of freedom. The relationship between the one-week attempt window mentioned initially and the two-week window used in analyses is unclear.
issues.quote: The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced.

issues.description: Despite acknowledging that 'numerous aspects of this research were exploratory by nature,' the study does not mention pre-registration. The OSF link provided appears to contain study materials but not a pre-registered analysis plan. Given the large number of outcome variables and the exploratory nature of many analyses, pre-registration would have been valuable for distinguishing confirmatory from exploratory findings.
issues.quote: Numerous aspects of this research were exploratory by nature.

issues.subcategory: Substantial data loss not fully characterized
issues.description: Of 293 episodes collected, only 134 (46%) had SMS data. Of 33 participants, only 27 contributed SMS data. The reasons for missing data (encryption issues, lack of cloud backups, new phones) are described qualitatively but not quantified systematically. Whether data missingness was related to episode type, recency, or participant characteristics is not examined, raising concerns about selection bias in the analyzed sample.
issues.quote: a number of iPhone users had encryption settings on their phones that prevented third-party iPhone software from accessing text data

issues.description: The study uses language suggesting causal or predictive relationships (e.g., 'predicted suicide attempt,' 'markers of suicide risk,' 'digital biomarkers') when the design is retrospective and correlational. The within-subjects comparisons identify associations between episode type and language features but cannot establish that language changes cause or reliably predict suicide attempts.
issues.quote: Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk.

issues.subcategory: Mismatch between first-person pronoun use and rumination
issues.description: The study equates first-person singular pronoun use with rumination and self-focus, but first-person pronouns serve many functions in communication beyond reflecting rumination (e.g., making plans, expressing preferences, narrating events). The construct validity of this operationalization is questionable, particularly in the context of SMS messages which are often brief and conversational.
issues.quote: we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of rumination) was greater prior to suicide attempts

issues.subcategory: Power analysis based on between-subjects effect sizes for within-subjects design
issues.description: The power analysis used effect sizes from between-subjects studies (d=0.88-1.52) to estimate power for a within-subjects design. The authors acknowledge this mismatch but proceed with the assumption of large effects. Within-subjects effect sizes for these constructs are unknown and could be substantially smaller, making the power analysis unreliable.
issues.quote: though no prior studies have examined within-subjects differences, which may or may not vary substantially from between-subjects comparisons

issues.subcategory: Sadness significant in Analysis 1 but not Analysis 2, and vice versa for anger
issues.description: Sadness was the only significant finding in Analysis 1 (means) but was non-significant in Analysis 2 (slopes; p=.721). Conversely, anger was non-significant in Analysis 1 (p=.694) but significant in Analysis 2 (p=.049). While these are different analyses testing different things, the pattern is not discussed—particularly why sadness would show mean differences but no temporal change, while anger shows temporal change but no mean differences.
issues.quote: Sadness (sad) χ²=8.74, p=.033 [Table 2] ... Sadness (sad) χ²=1.33, p=.721 [Table 3]

issues.description: The study reports 189,478 total messages but does not report the distribution of message lengths (word counts), which is critical given that LIWC scores were converted to proportions. Very short messages (e.g., 1-2 words) would produce extreme proportion values (0 or 1) that could unduly influence the models. No information about filtering or minimum word count thresholds is provided.
issues.quote: 189,478 text messages were collected and analyzed, ranging between on average about 1,200-1,600 text messages per episode

issues.description: Participants were recruited through a multi-stage screening process from a university participant pool, requiring them to have accessible text data from before their suicide attempt, minimal current suicidality, and willingness to share private communications. This creates substantial selection bias—participants who are willing and able to share their text messages may differ systematically from the broader population of suicide attempters.
issues.quote: participants were excluded if they did not have access to at least one data service type (e.g., text messages, Facebook) dating back to before their most recent suicide attempt

issues.subcategory: Degrees of freedom inconsistency in Table 2
issues.description: Table 2 lists two 'df' columns both showing '3' for all tests. For Wald chi-square tests of a 4-level factor, 3 df is correct for the numerator, but the second df column appears redundant or erroneous. If this was intended to represent denominator df, the value should differ and would depend on the random effects structure.
issues.quote: 1st-person pronouns – singular (i) | χ²=1.62 | 3 | 3 | .656

issues.description: The same experimenter who conducted the interview and classified episodes also performed the data analysis. There is no mention of blinding or independent verification of episode classifications. Given that episode classification is the foundation of the entire analysis, lack of blinding or inter-rater reliability assessment is a concern.
issues.quote: participants were interviewed by the experimenter and asked to identify a number of episodes... Recruitment and data collection were performed by J.J.G... J.J.G. performed the data analysis

issues.subcategory: Death words omnibus significant but no pairwise comparisons significant
issues.description: The omnibus test for the death words interaction was significant (χ²(3)=9.47, p=.024), but none of the pairwise comparisons involving attempt episodes reached significance (ps=.067-.739). This suggests the significant omnibus effect may be driven by differences between non-attempt episode types rather than differences involving attempts, yet the authors do not clearly state this or explore which comparison drove the omnibus effect.
issues.quote: there were no significant differences in change over time for attempt compared to all other episodes (zs=0.33-1.83, ps=.067-.739)
